H1.text: A tomato. A brinjal. A potato.

H2.text: One is red, one is purple, and one grows under the soil. Yet all three come from the same plant family.

H3.text: Aarav loves short codes. He is aiming for JEE, and he knows water is H two O. He asked: can a whole flower be written in one line like that?

H4.text: It can. Botanists write a floral formula, a one line code for a flower.

H5.text: By the end, you will read and write a floral formula, and use it to describe the potato family, Solanaceae.

D1.text: First, how does a botanist describe a flowering plant?

D2.text: In a fixed order. First its habit and its roots, stem and leaves. Then its flowers and their parts.

D3.text: The flower is written as a floral formula, and drawn as a floral diagram.

D4.text: In a floral diagram, a dot on top shows the mother axis, the stem the flower grows from. Then come the rings, from the calyx outside to the gynoecium in the centre.

Z1.text: Now, the code. Each part of the flower gets a symbol.

Z2.text: Br means the flower has a bract, a small leaf at its base. A circle with a cross means actinomorphic, a flower you can cut into two equal halves through any plane through its centre. A percent sign means zygomorphic, only one plane works.

Z3.text: K is the calyx, the whorl of sepals. C is the corolla, the whorl of petals. P is the perianth, used when sepals and petals look alike.

Z4.text: A is the androecium, the stamens. G is the gynoecium, the carpels. A line under the G number means a superior ovary. A line above it means an inferior ovary.

Z5.text: A number in brackets means the parts are fused, joined together. A line drawn above two symbols means adhesion, one whorl joined to another.

P1.text: Now let's decode one real formula, for the potato family, and build its floral diagram ring by ring.

P2.text: Step one. A circle with a cross, and the bisexual sign. The flower is actinomorphic, and has both stamens and a pistil.

P3.text: Step two. K five in brackets. Five sepals, joined. They stay on, even on the fruit, so they are persistent. Look at the green cap on a brinjal.

P4.text: Step three. C five in brackets. Five petals, also joined.

P5.text: Step four. A five, with a line joining it to C. Five stamens, fixed on the petals. They are epipetalous.

P6.text: Step five. G two in brackets, with a line below. Two fused carpels in a superior ovary, with two rooms. A swollen placenta carries many ovules. That is axile placentation.

C1.text: Now meet the family itself. Solanaceae is called the potato family.

C2.text: The plants are mostly herbs and shrubs, rarely small trees. The leaves are simple and alternate, with a net of veins.

C3.text: In potato, a stem grows under the soil. The potato we eat is a stem, not a root.

C4.text: The fruits are berries or capsules, with many seeds that keep their endosperm.

C5.text: This family feeds us. Tomato, brinjal and potato are food. Chilli is a spice. Belladonna and ashwagandha give medicine, tobacco is fumigatory, and petunia is grown for its flowers.

V1.text: Two code marks get mixed up. Brackets show fusion, parts of the same whorl joined, like five sepals in one cup.

V2.text: A line drawn above two symbols shows adhesion, parts of different whorls joined, like stamens fixed on petals.

V3.text: A line under the G number means a superior ovary, sitting above the other parts, as in brinjal. A line above means an inferior ovary, as in guava.

V4.text: Your turn. A formula shows C five in brackets, and a line joining C to A. Which mark shows adhesion? Pause and decide.

V5.text: The line! It joins stamens to petals, two different whorls. The brackets show fusion inside one whorl.

T1.text: Remember this. Brackets mean joined in the same whorl. A line means joined to another whorl.

W1.text: Now, a worked example. Let's write the formula of a makoi flower, Solanum nigrum, from what we see.

W2.text: The flower looks the same all round, and has both sexes. Circle with a cross, and the bisexual sign.

W3.text: Five sepals, joined. K five in brackets.

W4.text: Five petals, joined. C five in brackets.

W5.text: Five stamens on the petals. A five, with a line to C.

W6.text: Two fused carpels, and the ovary is superior. G two in brackets, with a line below.

W7.text: Put it together, and one line describes the whole flower.

X2.text: Many students think a line drawn above the symbols means fusion.

X3.text: But fusion is shown by brackets. The line above shows adhesion, one whorl joined to another, like stamens on petals.

E1.text: Where is this asked? As formula reading: what a floral formula tells you, or which family a description belongs to.

Q1.text: Exam level now. Which statement about Solanaceae is correct? Pause and solve.

A2.text: The line joining A to C shows epipetalous stamens, and the line below G shows a superior ovary.

A3.text: The ovary has two rooms with axile placentation, and the five sepals are joined and persistent.

Y2.text: One. What does a circle with a cross mean in a floral formula?

Y3.text: Two. How is adhesion shown in a floral formula?
